DOMAIN NAME DISPUTE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET AND THE DOMAIN NAME AT ISSUE
This information sheet concerns a domain name dispute involving Acme, Inc., who owns or claims rights in the mark described as: ACME (word mark), used on or in connection with: consumer electronics. The domain name at issue is acme-electronics.com, currently shown in publicly available registration records as registered to Jordan Lee. Acme, Inc. is preparing this information for possible use in a demand communication, an administrative dispute proceeding, or a civil action, and identifies October 1, 2026 as a date by which Acme, Inc. is seeking a response or resolution. This description reflects Acme, Inc.'s current understanding of the registration and use of the domain name. It is not a judicial or administrative finding, and nothing in this information sheet states that any court or dispute-resolution panel has determined that Jordan Lee's registration or use of the domain name violates any right of Acme, Inc.

THE ACPA'S CORE CAUSE OF ACTION: BAD-FAITH INTENT TO PROFIT FROM A DOMAIN NAME
A federal statute, commonly called the Anticybersquatting Consumer Protection Act (ACPA), creates civil liability for a person who has a bad faith intent to profit from a mark and who registers, traffics in, or uses a domain name that meets one of two distinct tests, depending on the mark. Where the mark is distinctive (but not necessarily famous) at the time the domain name is registered, the domain name must be identical or confusingly similar to that mark. Where the mark is famous at that time, the standard is broader: the domain name must be identical or confusingly similar to the mark, or dilutive of it — dilution alone is sufficient for a famous mark, but the statute does not extend the dilution-alone route to a mark that is merely distinctive without also being famous. Both bad-faith intent and one of these domain-name tests must be shown; neither alone is sufficient under this provision. The statute also limits who can be held liable for "using" a domain name under this cause of action: only the domain name registrant or that registrant's authorized licensee, not, for example, a web host or other third party merely providing services to the registrant.

  "in the case of a mark that is distinctive at the time of registration of the domain name, is identical or confusingly similar to that mark"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(1)(A)(ii)(I) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, ACPA — identical-or-confusingly-similar test for a distinctive mark (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1125)
  "in the case of a famous mark that is famous at the time of registration of the domain name, is identical or confusingly similar to or dilutive of that mark"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(1)(A)(ii)(II) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, ACPA — identical, confusingly similar, or dilutive test for a famous mark (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1125)
  "A person shall be liable for using a domain name under subparagraph (A) only if that person is the domain name registrant or that registrant’s authorized licensee."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(1)(D) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, ACPA — liability for "using" a domain name limited to the registrant or its authorized licensee (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1125)
  Known gap: This is federal law (the Lanham Act, applicable nationwide), used as real evidence of the ACPA's core statutory elements — not a claim that any specific domain name registration or use described on this sheet involves bad-faith intent, or that any specific mark is distinctive or famous, all of which this clause does not resolve. This clause quotes three passages from the same statutory paragraph, 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(1)(A) (the bad-faith-intent language and the two domain-name tests), plus one passage from the same paragraph's subparagraph (D) (the who-can-be-liable limitation); all four quotes are from a single statutory paragraph, 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(1), and are not independent corroborating sources of each other. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific registration or use of a domain name violates any right, and completing this information sheet does not itself send any demand letter or file any lawsuit or administrative complaint.

THE ACPA'S STATUTORY BAD-FAITH FACTORS AND ITS FAIR-USE SAFE HARBOR
The ACPA does not leave "bad faith intent to profit" undefined for a court to construe from nothing: the statute lists nine specific factors a court may consider, expressly stating that this list is illustrative and not exhaustive ("factors such as, but not limited to"). Among the statutory factors are the domain name registrant's own trademark or other intellectual property rights, if any, in the domain name; the registrant's prior use, if any, of the domain name in connection with a bona fide offering of goods or services; the registrant's bona fide noncommercial or fair use of the mark in a site accessible under the domain name; the registrant's intent to divert consumers from the mark owner's online location to a site that could harm the goodwill represented by the mark, for commercial gain or with intent to tarnish or disparage the mark, by creating a likelihood of confusion as to source, sponsorship, affiliation, or endorsement; and the registrant's offer to transfer, sell, or otherwise assign the domain name to the mark owner or a third party for financial gain, without having used, or having an intent to use, the domain name in a bona fide offering of goods or services. The statute also states an express limit on all of this: bad faith intent shall not be found in any case in which the court determines that the registrant believed, and had reasonable grounds to believe, that use of the domain name was a fair use or otherwise lawful.

ACPA REMEDIES: COURT-ORDERED TRANSFER OR CANCELLATION, AND STATUTORY DAMAGES PER DOMAIN NAME
Where a violation of the ACPA's cause of action is established in a civil action, the statute authorizes a court to order the forfeiture or cancellation of the domain name, or the transfer of the domain name to the owner of the mark — a remedy aimed at the domain name itself rather than solely at the registrant. Separately, the statute gives a mark owner the option to recover statutory damages instead of actual damages and profits, specifically for a violation of the ACPA's cyberpiracy provision: an award of not less than $1,000 and not more than $100,000 per domain name, in an amount the court considers just, elected by the plaintiff at any time before final judgment. This statutory-damages figure and election right apply specifically to ACPA violations; they are a distinct remedy from the general profits/damages/costs framework that applies to other Lanham Act violations such as ordinary infringement or dilution.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In any civil action involving the registration, trafficking, or use of a domain name under this paragraph, a court may order the forfeiture or cancellation of the domain name or the transfer of the domain name to the owner of the mark."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(1)(C) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, ACPA — court-ordered forfeiture, cancellation, or transfer of the domain name (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1125)
  "In a case involving a violation of section 1125(d)(1) of this title, the plaintiff may elect, at any time before final judgment is rendered by the trial court, to recover, instead of actual damages and profits, an award of statutory damages in the amount of not less than $1,000 and not more than $100,000 per domain name, as the court considers just."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1117(d) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, statutory damages of $1,000 to $100,000 per domain name for an ACPA violation (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1117)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the remedies the ACPA itself authorizes — not a claim that a court would order any particular remedy, or award any particular dollar amount within the statutory range, for any specific domain name registration or use described on this sheet, all of which this clause does not resolve and which depends on facts and judicial discretion this clause does not evaluate. This clause cites two different statutory sections that together form the ACPA's coordinated remedial scheme rather than two independent corroborating sources: 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(1)(C) (the forfeiture/cancellation/transfer remedy, located within the cyberpiracy provision itself) and 15 U.S.C. § 1117(d) (the statutory-damages election, which by its own text applies specifically "[i]n a case involving a violation of section 1125(d)(1)"). This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific registration or use of a domain name violates the ACPA or any other right, and completing this information sheet does not itself send any demand letter or file any lawsuit.

THE ACPA'S IN REM OPTION WHEN THE DOMAIN NAME REGISTRANT CANNOT BE SUED DIRECTLY
The ACPA includes a second, distinct procedural route beyond an ordinary civil action against a person: a mark owner may file an in rem civil action against the domain name itself, in the judicial district where the domain name registrar, registry, or other domain name authority that registered or assigned the domain name is located, if the domain name violates a right of the owner of a mark registered with the Patent and Trademark Office, or a right protected under the statute's false-designation-of-origin or dilution provisions, and the court finds that the mark owner either cannot obtain personal jurisdiction over a person who would have been a defendant in an ordinary civil action, or, through due diligence, was unable to find such a person after sending notice to the registrant's postal and e-mail address on file and publishing notice of the action as the court directs. This route exists precisely for situations — common in domain disputes — where the registrant is anonymous, has supplied false contact information, or is outside the court's personal jurisdiction. The remedies available in an in rem action are narrower than in an ordinary civil action: the statute limits them to a court order for the forfeiture or cancellation of the domain name, or its transfer to the mark owner; no monetary damages are available in an in rem action, consistent with the fact that no person is a defendant in it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The owner of a mark may file an in rem civil action against a domain name in the judicial district in which the domain name registrar, domain name registry, or other domain name authority that registered or assigned the domain name is located if"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(2)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, ACPA — in rem civil action against a domain name (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1125)
  "the domain name violates any right of the owner of a mark registered in the Patent and Trademark Office, or protected under subsection (a) or (c)"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(2)(A)(i) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, ACPA in rem action — underlying rights that can trigger the action (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1125)
  "The remedies in an in rem action under this paragraph shall be limited to a court order for the forfeiture or cancellation of the domain name or the transfer of the domain name to the owner of the mark."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(2)(D)(i) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, ACPA in rem action — remedies limited to forfeiture, cancellation, or transfer (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1125)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that this in rem procedural option and its jurisdictional prerequisites exist, and of the narrower remedies the statute allows in that posture — not a claim that in rem jurisdiction would be available for any specific domain name or registrant described on this sheet, which depends on facts (such as whether personal jurisdiction exists or due diligence was exercised) this clause does not evaluate. This clause quotes two passages from the same statutory paragraph, 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(2) (subparagraphs (A) and (D)(i)); they are not independent sources. This clause reports, without resolving, an open interpretive point: the in rem provision's own text cross-references a violation of rights protected under a registered mark or under subsection (a) (false designation of origin) or subsection (c) (dilution), rather than in terms repeating the "bad faith intent to profit" language used in the in personam cause of action at 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(1)(A); whether and how courts have required a showing equivalent to that bad-faith element in an in rem case is a case-law question this clause does not resolve, because a CourtListener case-law search on this point returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (daily quota exhausted) this session before any case could be retrieved. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that in rem jurisdiction would be available for any specific domain name, and completing this information sheet does not itself file any lawsuit.

FEDERAL COURT REVIEW AFTER A DOMAIN NAME IS SUSPENDED, DISABLED, OR TRANSFERRED UNDER A REGISTRAR'S ANTI-CYBERSQUATTING POLICY
Separately from the ACPA's own cause of action, federal trademark law addresses what happens when a domain name registrar, registry, or other domain name authority itself takes action against a domain name — refusing to register it, removing it, transferring it, temporarily disabling it, or permanently canceling it — under the registrar's own reasonable policy prohibiting registration of a domain name that is identical to, confusingly similar to, or dilutive of another's mark. Where a domain name registrant's domain name has been suspended, disabled, or transferred under such a policy, the statute gives that registrant a route back into federal court: upon notice to the mark owner, the registrant may file a civil action to establish that the registrant's registration or use of the domain name is not unlawful, and the court may grant injunctive relief, including reactivation of the domain name or its transfer back to the registrant. This means a private, registrar-level or administrative dispute outcome adverse to a domain name registrant is not necessarily the end of the matter: this statute gives the registrant an avenue to seek reversal in federal court.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "the implementation of a reasonable policy by such registrar, registry, or authority prohibiting the registration of a domain name that is identical to, confusingly similar to, or dilutive of another’s mark"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1114(2)(D)(ii)(II) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, registrar/registry safe harbor for implementing a reasonable anti-cybersquatting policy (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1114)
  "A domain name registrant whose domain name has been suspended, disabled, or transferred under a policy described under clause (ii)(II) may, upon notice to the mark owner, file a civil action to establish that the registration or use of the domain name by such registrant is not unlawful under this chapter. The court may grant injunctive relief to the domain name registrant, including the reactivation of the domain name or transfer of the domain name to the domain name registrant."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1114(2)(D)(v) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, registrant's right to federal court review after suspension, disabling, or transfer under such a policy (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1114)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that this specific statutory route back into federal court exists for a registrant whose domain name was suspended, disabled, or transferred under a registrar's or registry's own anti-cybersquatting policy — not a claim that this route would succeed for any specific domain name or registrant described on this sheet. This clause quotes two passages from the same statutory paragraph, 15 U.S.C. § 1114(2)(D) (subparagraphs (ii)(II) and (v)); they are not independent sources. Important limitation of this clause, disclosed here rather than glossed over: this document's research task asked whether this provision specifically overrides or interacts with ICANN's Uniform Domain-Name Dispute-Resolution Policy (UDRP), and, if verifiable, to include UDRP's own three-element test as a separate clause. Neither could be verified this session. Direct fetch attempts to icann.org and to wipo.int both failed with a network-egress-policy block (the proxy returned "CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403" for both hosts, confirmed by direct testing, not merely assumed), and a Wayback Machine mirror attempt (web.archive.org) was blocked the same way. A CourtListener case-law search for a federal opinion quoting the UDRP or discussing its relationship to this statute was attempted and returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error ("Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") before any case could be retrieved. Consequently: the quotations above are strictly to the statutory text itself, which describes a "reasonable policy... prohibiting the registration of a domain name that is identical to, confusingly similar to, or dilutive of another's mark" without naming the UDRP or any other specific policy; this clause does not assert that the UDRP is the policy the statute describes (although that identification is common outside this document, it was not verified from a primary or judicially-quoted source this session); and this document accordingly omits any separate clause purporting to state UDRP's own three-element test, rather than including one with an unverified or placeholder citation. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific domain name registrant is entitled to reactivation or transfer of any domain name, and completing this information sheet does not itself file any lawsuit.

DOMAIN NAME DISPUTE RESERVATION OF RIGHTS AND SIGNATURE
Nothing in this information sheet is a complete statement of the facts, claims, defenses, or legal theories available to Acme, Inc. or to Jordan Lee with respect to the domain name acme-electronics.com. Nothing in this information sheet waives or limits any right or remedy either party may have, all of which are expressly reserved, whether or not specifically mentioned above. This information sheet is not a lawsuit, an administrative complaint, and does not itself commence any court action or dispute-resolution proceeding.

expectedJSON.body: The ACPA includes a second, distinct procedural route beyond an ordinary civil action against a person: a mark owner may file an in rem civil action against the domain name itself, in the judicial district where the domain name registrar, registry, or other domain name authority that registered or assigned the domain name is located, if the domain name violates a right of the owner of a mark registered with the Patent and Trademark Office, or a right protected under the statute's false-designation-of-origin or dilution provisions, and the court finds that the mark owner either cannot obtain personal jurisdiction over a person who would have been a defendant in an ordinary civil action, or, through due diligence, was unable to find such a person after sending notice to the registrant's postal and e-mail address on file and publishing notice of the action as the court directs. This route exists precisely for situations — common in domain disputes — where the registrant is anonymous, has supplied false contact information, or is outside the court's personal jurisdiction. The remedies available in an in rem action are narrower than in an ordinary civil action: the statute limits them to a court order for the forfeiture or cancellation of the domain name, or its transfer to the mark owner; no monetary damages are available in an in rem action, consistent with the fact that no person is a defendant in it.

This clause reports, without resolving, an open interpretive point: the in rem provision's own text cross-references a violation of rights protected under a registered mark or under subsection (a) (false designation of origin) or subsection (c) (dilution), rather than in terms repeating the "bad faith intent to profit" language used in the in personam cause of action at 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(1)(A); whether and how courts have required a showing equivalent to that bad-faith element in an in rem case is a case-law question this clause does not resolve, because a CourtListener case-law search on this point returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (daily quota exhausted) this session before any case could be retrieved. expectedJSON.body: Separately from the ACPA's own cause of action, federal trademark law addresses what happens when a domain name registrar, registry, or other domain name authority itself takes action against a domain name — refusing to register it, removing it, transferring it, temporarily disabling it, or permanently canceling it — under the registrar's own reasonable policy prohibiting registration of a domain name that is identical to, confusingly similar to, or dilutive of another's mark. Where a domain name registrant's domain name has been suspended, disabled, or transferred under such a policy, the statute gives that registrant a route back into federal court: upon notice to the mark owner, the registrant may file a civil action to establish that the registrant's registration or use of the domain name is not unlawful, and the court may grant injunctive relief, including reactivation of the domain name or its transfer back to the registrant. This means a private, registrar-level or administrative dispute outcome adverse to a domain name registrant is not necessarily the end of the matter: this statute gives the registrant an avenue to seek reversal in federal court.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, registrar/registry safe harbor for implementing a reasonable anti-cybersquatting policy
citations.quote: the implementation of a reasonable policy by such registrar, registry, or authority prohibiting the registration of a domain name that is identical to, confusingly similar to, or dilutive of another’s mark

citations.cite: U.S. Code, registrant's right to federal court review after suspension, disabling, or transfer under such a policy
citations.quote: A domain name registrant whose domain name has been suspended, disabled, or transferred under a policy described under clause (ii)(II) may, upon notice to the mark owner, file a civil action to establish that the registration or use of the domain name by such registrant is not unlawful under this chapter. The court may grant injunctive relief to the domain name registrant, including the reactivation of the domain name or transfer of the domain name to the domain name registrant.

This clause quotes two passages from the same statutory paragraph, 15 U.S.C. § 1114(2)(D) (subparagraphs (ii)(II) and (v)); they are not independent sources.
